resources.label: PhET: Forces and Motion Basics
resources.note: The Net Force tab: a tug of war where the resultant is shown as you add people.

tips.title: Weight is a force, mass is not
tips.body: $W = mg$. Mass is in kilograms and never changes; weight is in **newtons** and depends on the gravitational field strength. On the Moon the mass is the same and the weight is smaller.

tips.title: Give the direction too
tips.body: A resultant of *100 N* scores less than *100 N to the right*. A resultant force is a **vector**, so the direction is part of the answer.

tips.title: Contact needs touching
tips.body: **Contact** forces need the objects to touch: friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact. **Non-contact** forces act at a distance: gravity, magnetism, electrostatic. Sorting them is a one-mark question worth having ready.

steps.title: A force is a push or a pull, and a vector
steps.body:
A **force** is a push or a pull on an object caused by it interacting with something else. Forces are measured in **newtons (N)**.

A force is a **vector**: it has a size and a direction, so it is drawn as an arrow. The arrow's length shows the size and its direction shows the direction. Scalars, such as mass, time and energy, have no direction and get no arrow.

The diagram shows one force on a box: a 40 N push to the right. Everything else in this topic is about what happens when there is more than one arrow.

visuals.alt: A box with a single arrow pointing right labelled push 40 N, and the resultant written underneath as 40 N to the right

check.prompt: Which of these is a scalar?
check.solution: Mass has a size but no direction: 5 kg is 5 kg whichever way you turn. Force, weight and acceleration all have a direction.

steps.title: Contact and non-contact forces
steps.body:
A **contact force** needs the two objects to touch: friction, air resistance, tension in a rope, and the normal contact force a surface pushes back with.

A **non-contact force** acts at a distance: gravity, magnetism, and the electrostatic force between charges.

The exam asks for one example of each, and for the *pair* of objects involved. Weight is the gravitational force between an object and the Earth: non-contact, even when the object is sitting on the ground.

visuals.alt: A table of contact forces, friction, air resistance, tension and normal contact force, beside non-contact forces, gravity, magnetic and electrostatic

check.prompt: Which force is a non-contact force?
check.solution: A magnet pulls a paperclip without touching it. The other three need contact.

steps.title: Weight is a force; mass is not
steps.body:
**Mass** is how much matter an object has, in kg. **Weight** is the force of gravity on it, in N. They are linked by the gravitational field strength $g$:

$$W = m\,g$$

On Earth $g = 9.8$ N/kg, so a 60 kg person weighs $60 \times 9.8 = 588$ N. This equation is a recall equation.

Weight acts from a single point called the **centre of mass**: for a regular shape, the middle. On a diagram, draw weight as one arrow from the centre, straight down. Weight is measured with a calibrated spring balance, sometimes called a newtonmeter.

visuals.alt: A card showing weight equals mass times gravitational field strength, with units N, kg and N/kg

check.prompt: Calculate the weight of a 60 kg person on Earth, where $g = 9.8$ N/kg.

steps.title: Same mass, different weight
steps.body: Mass does not change when you move somewhere else. Weight does, because $g$ does. On the Moon, $g$ is about 1.6 N/kg, so everything weighs about a sixth of what it does here, while its mass is unchanged. That is the whole point of keeping the two words apart.

visuals.problem: A 60 kg astronaut goes to the Moon, where $g = 1.6$ N/kg. What are their mass and weight there?

steps.text: Mass on the Moon: still **60 kg**
steps.note: mass is the amount of matter; it does not change

steps.text: Weight on the Moon: $W = m g = 60 \times 1.6 = 96$ N
The astronaut weighs about a sixth as much but is not any less massive
steps.note: easier to lift, just as hard to push

check.prompt: A 120 kg lunar rover is on the Moon, where $g = 1.6$ N/kg. Calculate its weight.

steps.title: The resultant force
steps.body:
When several forces act on one object, they can be replaced by a single force that has the same effect. That single force is the **resultant force**.

Forces along the same line simply add or subtract. A 300 N push forward and 200 N of friction backward give a resultant of $300 - 200 = 100$ N forward. Always give the size *and* the direction.

The diagram is a **free body diagram**: the object on its own, with every force on it drawn as an arrow from the object, and nothing else. Draw one before you calculate anything.

visuals.alt: A free body diagram of a crate with a 300 N push to the right and 200 N friction to the left, and the resultant force written as 100 N to the right

check.prompt: A sledge is pulled with a force of 90 N. Friction is 35 N. What is the resultant force?
check.skill: resultant of forces in a line
check.solution: $90 - 35 = 55$ N, in the direction of the pull.

steps.title: Balanced forces: resultant zero
steps.body:
If the resultant force is **zero**, the forces are **balanced**. A balanced object stays as it is: stationary if it was stationary, or moving at the same steady velocity if it was moving. Balanced does not mean stopped.

This car has thrust equal to drag and weight equal to the normal contact force from the road. The resultant is zero in both directions, so the car keeps its velocity.

That is the exam's favourite trap: a car at constant velocity has balanced forces, not a forward resultant.

visuals.alt: A free body diagram of a car with 500 N thrust to the right, 500 N drag to the left, 8000 N weight downwards and 8000 N normal contact force upwards, with the resultant written as zero, forces balanced

check.prompt: A lorry travels along a straight road at a steady 20 m/s. Which is true about the forces on it?
check.solution: Steady velocity means zero resultant: thrust equals the resistive forces. Forces still act; they cancel.
options: The forward force is larger than the resistive forces
The forces are balanced, so the resultant is zero
There are no forces acting on it
The resistive forces are larger than the forward force

steps.title: Work done: force times distance
steps.body:
When a force moves an object, **work** is done and energy is transferred:

$$W = F\,s$$

$W$ is work done in joules (J), $F$ the force in N, $s$ the distance moved *along the line of the force* in m. One joule is one newton metre: $1$ J $= 1$ N m. Recall this one too.

Pushing a box 4 m with a 50 N force does $50 \times 4 = 200$ J of work. Work done against friction heats things up, which is why brakes get hot. Carrying a bag along a flat corridor does no work on the bag in the physics sense, because the force is up and the movement is sideways.

visuals.alt: A card showing work done equals force times distance, with units J, N and m

check.prompt: A shopper pushes a trolley with a force of 50 N for 4 m. Calculate the work done.

steps.title: Two directions at once
steps.body: Deal with horizontal and vertical separately. The vertical forces usually balance for something on the ground, so the resultant comes from the horizontal pair. Write both lines even when one is zero: the examiner wants to see that you checked.

visuals.alt: A free body diagram of a van with 400 N thrust right, 150 N resistive force left, 8000 N weight down and 8000 N contact force up, and the resultant written as 250 N to the right

visuals.problem: Find the resultant force on the van.

steps.text: Vertical: $8000$ N up and $8000$ N down, resultant $0$
steps.note: the road holds it up exactly
the two horizontal forces are in a line

steps.text: Resultant: **250 N forwards**, so the van accelerates

check.prompt: A boat's engine pushes it forward with 900 N. Water resistance is 650 N. Its weight of 12 000 N is balanced by upthrust. What is the resultant force?
check.solution: Vertical forces balance. Horizontal: $900 - 650 = 250$ N forwards.

steps.title: Your turn: weight against mass
steps.body:
Drag the mass. The graph is $W = m g$ with $g = 9.8$ N/kg: a straight line through the origin, because weight is directly proportional to mass. The gradient of the line is $g$.

On the Moon the line would be much shallower, with gradient 1.6 N/kg. A spring balance reads weight; a balance that compares against known masses reads mass, and would give the same reading on the Moon.

visuals.fallback: A straight line through the origin with gradient 9.8: 98 N at 10 kg, 490 N at 50 kg and 980 N at 100 kg.

check.prompt: Read from the line or calculate: what is the weight of 45 kg on Earth?

steps.title: Going deeper: forces at an angle
steps.body:
Higher tier only: when two forces are not in a line, add them with a **scale drawing**. Draw the first force to scale, draw the second starting from the head of the first, then draw the resultant from the start of the first to the head of the second. Measure its length and convert back with your scale.

A 4 N force east and a 3 N force north give a resultant of **5 N**, at 37° north of east. The same triangle works backwards, which is called **resolving**: any single force can be split into two components at right angles, usually horizontal and vertical, and the object behaves exactly as if only the two components acted.

If forces drawn head to tail form a **closed** shape, the resultant is zero: the object is in equilibrium.

visuals.alt: A vector diagram: a 4 N arrow to the right, then a 3 N arrow upwards from its head, with a dashed resultant of 5 N drawn from the start to the final head

check.prompt: Two forces act on a ring: 6 N east and 8 N north. What is the size of the resultant force?
check.solution: A scale drawing gives a 6, 8, 10 right-angled triangle, so the resultant is 10 N. Pythagoras confirms it: $\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = 10$.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A force is a push or a pull, in newtons, and a vector: draw it as an arrow.
- Contact forces need touching (friction, drag, tension, normal contact); non-contact forces act at a distance (gravity, magnetic, electrostatic).
- $W = m g$: weight in N, mass in kg, $g = 9.8$ N/kg on Earth. Mass never changes; weight depends on $g$. Weight acts at the centre of mass.
- The resultant force is the single force with the same effect as all the forces together. Zero resultant means balanced: stationary, or steady velocity.
- $W = F s$: work done in joules, one newton metre each.
- Higher: add forces at an angle head to tail, to scale; resolve a force into two components at right angles.

equations.equation: add forces in a line; head to tail at an angle

questions.prompt: Which of these is a non-contact force?
questions.solution: Gravity acts at a distance; the other three need the objects to touch.

questions.prompt: Calculate the weight of a 5 kg bag of potatoes on Earth. $g = 9.8$ N/kg.
The free body diagram shows a box pushed to the right with 250 N while friction is 100 N. Calculate the resultant force.
questions.skill: resultant of forces in a line

visual.alt: A box with 250 N push to the right and 100 N friction to the left

questions.solution: Weight is a force, so it is measured in **newtons (N)**. Kilograms are the unit of mass.

questions.prompt: A removal worker pushes a piano 15 m across a floor with a steady force of 120 N. Calculate the work done.
An astronaut travels from Earth to the Moon. Which is correct?
questions.solution: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change. Weight is $m g$, and $g$ on the Moon is about 1.6 N/kg, so weight falls.
options: Mass stays the same and weight decreases
Mass decreases and weight stays the same
Mass and weight both stay the same

questions.prompt: A person weighs 735 N on Earth, where $g = 9.8$ N/kg. Calculate their mass.
questions.solution: $W = m g$, so $m = W \div g = 735 \div 9.8 = 75$ kg.

questions.prompt: A model rocket has a weight of 800 N. Its engine produces 1200 N of thrust upwards. Calculate the resultant force at the moment of launch.
questions.skill: resultant of forces in a line

visual.alt: A rocket with 1200 N thrust upwards and 800 N weight downwards

questions.prompt: What is meant by the centre of mass of an object?
questions.solution: The centre of mass is the single point through which the whole weight of the object can be considered to act. For a regular shape it is the middle, but the definition is about where the weight acts.
options: The point where the object is heaviest
The point where the object's weight can be taken to act
The point at the exact middle of the object
The point where the object touches the ground

questions.prompt: A cyclist does 600 J of work against air resistance over 12 m. Calculate the average force of air resistance.
questions.solution: $W = F s$, so $F = W \div s = 600 \div 12 = 50$ N.

questions.prompt: Two tugs pull a ship. One pulls with 6 kN due east and the other with 8 kN due north. Use a vector diagram or calculation to find the size of the resultant force, in kN.
questions.solution: Draw 6 kN east, then 8 kN north from its head. The resultant closes the triangle: $\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ kN, at about 53° north of east.

markScheme.description: forces drawn head to tail, or $6^2 + 8^2$

visual.alt: A vector diagram with a 6 kN arrow to the right and an 8 kN arrow upwards from its head, resultant not drawn

questions.prompt: A boat is pulled by two ropes. One rope pulls with a force of 300 N due north and the other with 400 N due east. Describe how to find the resultant force using a scale drawing, and give its size and direction.
questions.solution: Choose a scale, such as 1 cm to 50 N. Draw the 300 N force as a 6 cm arrow pointing north. From the head of that arrow draw the 400 N force as an 8 cm arrow pointing east. Draw the resultant from the tail of the first arrow to the head of the second. Measure it: 10 cm, which is 500 N. Measure the angle with a protractor: about 53° east of north. Pythagoras confirms $\sqrt{300^2 + 400^2} = 500$ N.

markScheme.description: draws the first force to scale in the correct direction
draws the second force from the head of the first
draws the resultant from the first tail to the last head
direction about 53° east of north (or 37° north of east)

criteria.text: States a suitable scale, such as 1 cm to 50 N
Draws the 300 N force to scale pointing north
Draws the 400 N force to scale starting from the head of the first arrow
Draws the resultant from the start of the first arrow to the head of the second, and measures it
Direction about 53° east of north, measured with a protractor

questions.modelAnswer: Choose a scale, for example 1 cm represents 50 N. Draw the 300 N force as an arrow 6 cm long pointing north. From the head of that arrow, draw the 400 N force as an arrow 8 cm long pointing east. The resultant is the arrow from the tail of the first force to the head of the second. Measuring it gives 10 cm, which at 50 N per cm is 500 N. Measuring the angle between the resultant and north with a protractor gives about 53°, so the resultant is 500 N at 53° east of north. Check: the triangle is 3, 4, 5, so Pythagoras gives 500 N.

questions.prompt: A child pulls a sledge with a 50 N force through a rope at 37° above the horizontal. A scale drawing resolves the force into components. Find the horizontal component of the force. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
questions.solution: Draw the 50 N force at 37° to scale, then drop a vertical line from its head to the horizontal; the horizontal component is the base of the triangle. It measures $50 \cos 37° = 39.9$ N, which is **40 N** to 2 s.f. The vertical component is 30 N, so the components make a 3, 4, 5 triangle.

markScheme.description: force drawn to scale at 37°, or $50 \cos 37°$
horizontal component taken as the base of the right-angled triangle

questions.prompt: A crane lifts a 250 kg load vertically at a steady speed. $g = 9.8$ N/kg. Show that the tension in the cable is 2450 N, and explain why it is not larger.
questions.solution: Weight $= m g = 250 \times 9.8 = 2450$ N downwards. Steady speed means zero resultant force, so the upward tension must equal the weight: 2450 N, as required. The tension is not larger because a larger tension would give a resultant force upwards and the load would accelerate, not move at steady speed.

markScheme.description: steady speed means the resultant force is zero
a larger tension would give an upward resultant and an acceleration

criteria.text: States that steady speed means zero resultant force (balanced forces)
So tension $=$ weight $= 2450$ N, as required
A larger tension would give an upward resultant force, so the load would accelerate upwards rather than rise steadily

questions.modelAnswer: The weight of the load is $W = m g = 250 \times 9.8 = 2450$ N, acting downwards. The load moves at a steady speed, so its velocity is not changing, which means the resultant force on it is zero. The only other force is the tension in the cable, acting upwards, so the tension must be equal to the weight: 2450 N. It is not larger because any extra tension would produce an upward resultant force, and the load would then accelerate upwards instead of rising at a steady speed.

questions.prompt: A car's engine provides a forward force of 600 N while resistive forces total 350 N. The car travels 40 m. Calculate the work done by the resultant force.
questions.solution: Resultant $= 600 - 350 = 250$ N. Work done $= F s = 250 \times 40 = 10000$ J. This is the energy transferred to the car's kinetic energy store.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of a scale drawing to find the resultant of two forces at an angle in order.
questions.solution: Scale first, then the two forces head to tail, then the resultant from start to finish, then measure and convert.

markScheme.description: second force from the head of the first
resultant from tail to head, then measure

items: Choose a scale and write it down
Draw the first force as an arrow of the right length and direction
Draw the second force starting from the head of the first
Draw the resultant from the tail of the first arrow to the head of the second
Measure the resultant's length and angle, and convert the length back using the scale

questions.prompt: A 40 kg probe has a weight of 148 N on the surface of Mars. Calculate the gravitational field strength on Mars.
questions.solution: $W = m g$, so $g = W \div m = 148 \div 40 = 3.7$ N/kg.

questions.prompt: A book rests on a table. Student A says: *there are no forces on the book, because it is not moving.* Student B says: *there are forces, but they cancel out.* Evaluate the two statements, using a free body diagram.
questions.skill: evaluating a claim about balanced forces
questions.solution: Student B is right. Two forces act on the book: its weight, downwards, from the Earth's gravity, and the normal contact force from the table, upwards. They are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the resultant force is zero. A zero resultant means the book's motion does not change: it stays at rest. Student A has confused *no resultant force* with *no forces*. If the table were removed the weight would still act and the book would fall, which shows the weight was there all along.

markScheme.description: names the normal contact force upwards from the table
equal size, opposite direction, so resultant zero
zero resultant means no change in motion, so it stays at rest
concludes B is right and A confuses no resultant with no forces

criteria.text: Weight acts downwards on the book
The table pushes upwards with a normal contact force
The two forces are equal and opposite, so the resultant is zero
Zero resultant force means the motion does not change, so the book stays still
Student B is correct; Student A has confused a zero resultant with no forces

questions.modelAnswer: Student B is correct. The free body diagram of the book shows two forces: the weight of the book acting downwards, which is the pull of the Earth's gravity, and the normal contact force from the table acting upwards. The two are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the resultant force on the book is zero. When the resultant force is zero the object's motion does not change, and since the book was at rest it stays at rest. Student A is wrong to say there are no forces: there are two, and they cancel. The difference matters, because if the table were taken away the weight would still act and the book would fall.

visual.alt: A free body diagram of a book with weight downwards and normal contact force upwards, equal in size

questions.prompt: A skydiver of mass 80 kg is falling at terminal velocity. $g = 9.8$ N/kg. The parachute opens and air resistance rises to 1200 N. Calculate the resultant force on the skydiver at that moment.
questions.solution: Weight $= 80 \times 9.8 = 784$ N downwards. Air resistance 1200 N upwards. Resultant $= 1200 - 784 = 416$ N **upwards**, so the skydiver decelerates.

examTechnique.body:
Force questions reward a habit: draw the free body diagram first, even when the question does not ask for one. Every arrow starts on the object, has a label and a size, and then the resultant is arithmetic. Say the direction of every resultant; a bare number loses the mark.

Keep mass and weight apart in your writing. Mass is kg and never changes; weight is N and is $m g$. If a question says *steady speed* or *at rest*, write *resultant force is zero* before anything else, because that sentence is usually a mark on its own. On Higher, the scale drawing needs a stated scale, arrows head to tail, and a measured length converted back.
examinerErrors: Giving a resultant force with no direction. *100 N* scores less than *100 N forwards*.
Saying a body at steady speed has a forward resultant force. Steady velocity means the resultant is zero.
Using kg as a unit of weight, or writing that mass changes on the Moon.
Drawing forces on a free body diagram that act on other objects, such as the push of the box on the floor.
Adding forces at an angle as if they were in a line: 3 N and 4 N at right angles give 5 N, not 7 N.
Using the distance moved rather than the distance along the line of the force when calculating work done.
Forgetting the scale, or drawing the second force from the tail of the first rather than its head.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer draws a labelled free body diagram before calculating, states that a body at rest or at constant velocity has zero resultant force, and gives every resultant with a direction. It keeps mass in kg and weight in N without slipping, rearranges $W = m g$ and $W = F s$ cleanly, and on Higher adds forces at an angle with a stated scale and head-to-tail arrows, checking a right-angled case with Pythagoras. In an evaluate question it separates *no resultant force* from *no forces* and says which student is right and why.
